traditions/alexandrian-orthodox/name: Greek Orthodox Patriarchate of Alexandria and All Africa
traditions/alexandrian-orthodox/summary: The Chalcedonian Patriarchate of Alexandria, which after 451 was a minority beside the Coptic Orthodox Church. Long the church of Greek communities in Egypt, in the twentieth century it gained a large African flock, beginning with the movement of Reuben Spartas in Uganda (1920s–1940s), and now has dioceses across sub-Saharan Africa.
traditions/alexandrian-orthodox/distinct: Claims St Mark as founder (shared with the Coptic Church)
Jurisdiction over the whole of Africa
Rapid growth through African mission (Kenya, Uganda, DR Congo, etc.)
Recognised the Orthodox Church of Ukraine (2019), after which Moscow created a rival African exarchate (2021)
traditions/alexandrian-orthodox/profile/: Holy Tradition, of which Scripture is the summit, interpreted through the seven ecumenical councils, the Fathers and the liturgy; the conciliar mind of the bishops in communion.
Salvation is theosis: union with God by grace through Christ in the Holy Spirit, received in baptism and lived out in faith, repentance, prayer and the sacramental life of the Church.
Seven principal Mysteries (baptism by triple immersion, chrismation, Eucharist, confession, ordination, marriage, holy unction), with infant communion; leavened bread in the Eucharist.
Expectation of Christ's return, the resurrection and judgement; prayer for the departed and the communion of saints; no doctrine of purgatory.
Pope and Patriarch of Alexandria (Theodore II since 2004) with a Holy Synod of metropolitans, many now African.
Byzantine rite in Greek, Arabic, English, French, Swahili and other African languages.
Old Testament from the Septuagint, including the books Protestants call deuterocanonical (anagignoskomena), and the 27-book New Testament.
traditions/alexandrian-orthodox/status: Active and growing in Africa; affected by the jurisdictional conflict with Moscow since 2021.
traditions/jerusalem-orthodox/summary: Raised to patriarchal rank at the Council of Chalcedon (451), the Patriarchate of Jerusalem is custodian, with the Latins and Armenians, of the principal Holy Places under the Ottoman 'Status Quo' arrangements. Its hierarchy is drawn largely from the Greek Brotherhood of the Holy Sepulchre, while most of its faithful are Arabic-speaking Palestinians and Jordanians — a long-standing source of tension. The autonomous Archdiocese of Sinai (St Catherine's Monastery) is connected with it.
traditions/jerusalem-orthodox/distinctiv: Guardian of the Church of the Holy Sepulchre and Bethlehem's Church of the Nativity
Holy Fire ceremony on Holy Saturday
Ottoman-era Status Quo regulating shared holy sites

traditions/serbian-orthodox/summary: Founded as an autocephalous archbishopric by St Sava in 1219, raised to a patriarchate at Peć in 1346, abolished by the Ottomans in 1766 and restored as a unified patriarchate in 1920. It is closely bound to Serbian national memory, including the Kosovo tradition, and suffered heavily in the Second World War and under communism.
traditions/serbian-orthodox/distinctives: St Sava's foundation and the 'Svetosavlje' ideal
Medieval monasteries in Kosovo (Dečani, Peć, Gračanica)
Recognised the Archbishopric of Ohrid (North Macedonia) in 2022, ending a long dispute
Disputes with the Montenegrin Orthodox movement

traditions/romanian-orthodox/summary: The Orthodox church of the Romanian people, the only large Orthodox church of Latin language and culture. Autocephalous since 1885 and a patriarchate since 1925, it survived communist control (1947–1989) with both compromise and martyrdom, and has grown institutionally since 1989, including a large diaspora in Italy and Spain.

traditions/bulgarian-orthodox/summary: The church that grew from the baptism of Khan Boris I (864) and the Slavonic literary school of Clement and Naum of Ohrid. A Bulgarian patriarchate existed in the medieval tsardoms; under the Ottomans it was absorbed into the Greek-led patriarchate. The Exarchate of 1870 led to a schism with Constantinople (1872–1945). The patriarchate was restored in 1953.

Rila Monastery and St John of Rila
Internal schism of 1992–2010 related to communist-era appointments

traditions/georgian-orthodox/summary: Rooted in the conversion of King Mirian III through St Nino (c. 337), the Georgian church became autocephalous under a Catholicos in late antiquity. Russia abolished its autocephaly in 1811; it was restored in 1917, recognised by Moscow in 1943 and by Constantinople in 1990. Under Patriarch Ilia II (from 1977) it has become Georgia's most trusted institution.

traditions/cypriot-orthodox/summary: The church of Cyprus traces its origin to the mission of Paul and Barnabas (Acts 13). The Council of Ephesus (431) upheld its independence from Antioch, and Emperor Zeno later confirmed its privileges after the discovery of the relics of Barnabas — including the archbishop's right to sign in red ink. Under Ottoman rule the archbishop became ethnarch of the Greek Cypriots; Archbishop Makarios III became the first president of the Republic of Cyprus (1960).
